ui.title: The Life and Teachings of Jesus
ui.desc: The life of Jesus from Part IV of The Urantia Book, retold as a single novel in 55 illustrated chapters, by Jay Han.
ui.og_title: The Life and Teachings of Jesus — The Story the Gospels Did Not Tell
intro.title: The Life and Teachings of Jesus
intro.sub: The Story the Gospels Did Not Tell · by Jay Han
intro.one: The Gospels tell us the events of only a few weeks of the life of Jesus.
intro.alt: Front cover of The Life and Teachings of Jesus
intro.meta2: Eight parts, fifty-five chapters · 55 color illustrations
intro.about1: What kind of boy grew up in the carpenter's home in Nazareth? How did the eldest son provide for his family after his father died? What did he see, learn, and endure in the nearly thirty years before his public ministry? Part IV of The Urantia Book, "The Life and Teachings of Jesus," fills that long silence with dates, places, and the names of the people who shared his life. This book retells that story so that it can be read from beginning to end like a single novel.
intro.about2: One principle has governed the writing. The events and dates, the persons and places, and above all the teachings of Jesus do not go beyond what Part IV of The Urantia Book records. No new events or words have been invented; the words of Jesus are quoted, wherever possible, exactly as they appear in the text. Fifty-five chapters, each opening with a color illustration newly painted for this book.
intro.list1.title: The Eight Parts
intro.list1.1: Part One, The Child of Nazareth: Gabriel's visit, the night in Bethlehem, the boy full of questions, and the Passover pilgrimage at twelve.
intro.list1.2: Part Two, The Hidden Years in Nazareth: the sudden death of Joseph, the eldest son as head of the family, Rebecca's love, and the day he left home.
intro.list1.3: Part Three, Walking the Mediterranean World: the journey with Gonod and Ganid, from Alexandria to Rome, Corinth, Athens, Ephesus, and Mesopotamia.
intro.list1.4: Part Four, The Fullness of Time: the Caspian caravan and Mount Hermon, John the Baptist, the baptism in the Jordan, the forty days, and the calling of the twelve.
intro.list1.5: Part Five, The Gospel of the Kingdom: Nicodemus, the woman at Jacob's well, teaching about prayer, healing at sundown, the women's corps, the parables by the sea, and the feeding of the five thousand.
intro.list1.6: Part Six, The Time of Sifting: the crisis at Capernaum, Peter's confession, the transfiguration, the seventy, the good Samaritan, Lazarus, and the lost son.
intro.list1.7: Part Seven, The Last Week in Jerusalem: the entry into the city, the last supper, the farewell discourses, Gethsemane, the trial, Golgotha, and the Sabbath in the tomb.
intro.list1.8: Part Eight, Resurrection and After: the empty tomb, the nineteen morontia appearances, the ascension and Pentecost, and an epilogue on the faith of Jesus.
intro.pre1: The Gospels tell us the events of only a few weeks of the life of Jesus. In what kind of home did he grow up? How did he provide for his family after his father died? What did he see, learn, and endure in the nearly thirty years before his public ministry? For a long time these questions had no answer. Part IV of *The Urantia Book*, “The Life and Teachings of Jesus,” fills that silence. The child born in a carpenter’s home in Nazareth grows up, travels the Mediterranean world, calls twelve men to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom of heaven, passes through the cross and the resurrection, and pours out the Spirit of Truth upon all flesh—and the whole of that life unfolds with dates, places, and the names of the people who shared it.
intro.pre2: Yet Part IV, as befits a record of revelation, is written in dense prose and at great length, and a first-time reader can find it hard to follow to the end. This book retells that story so that it can be read from beginning to end like a single novel.
intro.pre3: One principle has governed the writing. The events and dates, the persons and places, and above all the teachings of Jesus do not go beyond what Part IV of *The Urantia Book* records. No new events or words have been invented. What has been added is the landscape and atmosphere of each scene; long discourses and commentaries have been shortened; and the narrative has been joined so that it reads easily. The words of Jesus are quoted, wherever possible, exactly as they appear in the text. The illustration at the head of each chapter was newly painted for this book from the scenes the text describes.
intro.pre4: This book does not replace the original. If this story moves you, I hope that one day you will open Part IV of *The Urantia Book* for yourself. There, far more teachings and stories than these pages could hold are waiting for you.
ch00.title: The Decision Made in Heaven
ch00.b001: Salvington, on the Eve of the Bestowal
ch00.b002: On Salvington, the capital of the local universe of Nebadon, a single piece of news had gone out among the assembled hosts: Michael, the Creator Son who had made this universe, was about to depart on his final bestowal. Six times already he had bestowed himself after the similitude of six differing orders of his own intelligent creatures. To live such identical lives as he imposes upon the beings of his creation was part of the price every Creator Son must pay for the full and supreme sovereignty of his self-made universe. Only one bestowal remained, and it was the lowliest of all. He was to descend in the likeness of mortal flesh, the lowest order of his intelligent will creatures, and as a human being of the material realm to execute the final act in the drama of the acquirement of universe sovereignty.
ch00.b003: He need not have done it. At any moment throughout all past universe time, Michael could have asserted personal sovereignty as a Creator Son and ruled his universe after the manner of his own choosing. But he did not wish to rule Nebadon merely in his own isolated right. He desired to rise, through actual experience and in co-operative subordination to the Paradise Trinity, to that high place where he would be qualified to rule with perfect insight and wisdom. And so, in each bestowal, he had voluntarily subordinated himself to a different aspect of the will of Deity: on the first to the combined will of the Father, Son, and Spirit; on the second to the will of the Father and the Son; on the third to the Father and the Spirit; on the fourth to the Son and the Spirit; on the fifth to the Infinite Spirit; on the sixth to the Eternal Son. On the seventh and final bestowal, on Urantia, he would be subject to the will of the Universal Father. When it was done he would combine in his personal sovereignty the sevenfold will of the Paradise Creators with the understanding experience of his own creatures. His power would be unlimited because it derived from association with the Paradise Deities; his authority unquestioned because it was earned in the likeness of the creatures he ruled.
ch00.b004: The time had been chosen, and the planet too: Urantia, a small world disordered and disturbed by rebellion. Michael held the usual prebestowal conference with Gabriel, and then he presented himself before his elder brother and Paradise counselor, Immanuel, the Union of Days, ambassador of the Paradise Trinity to Nebadon. Into Immanuel’s keeping he gave all the powers of universe administration that had not already been conferred upon Gabriel. And just before Michael’s departure, Immanuel, in accepting the custody of the universe, proceeded to impart the bestowal counsel that would serve as Michael’s guide when he should presently grow up on Urantia as a mortal of the realm. This time he was acting on behalf of the Universal Father himself, and Michael could go with a quiet heart: Immanuel would exercise the full authority of the Father in his absence, and the Ancients of Days of the superuniverse had decreed the safety of his realm throughout the whole bestowal period.
ch00.b006: Immanuel’s words that day were long and solemn. He began by reminding his brother how different this bestowal would be from all that had gone before.
ch00.b008: Michael had voluntarily divested himself of all extraplanetary support and of every special assistance any creature of his own making might render. As his created sons of Nebadon are wholly dependent upon him for safe conduct throughout their universe careers, so now must he become wholly and unreservedly dependent upon his Paradise Father throughout the unrevealed vicissitudes of a mortal career. When it was over, he would know in very truth the full meaning of that faith-trust which he so unvaryingly required of all his creatures. Immanuel told him that he need be concerned with but one thing, “⟦Q 120:1.4⟧the unbroken communion between you and your Paradise Father.⟦/Q⟧” By the perfection of that relationship, the world of his bestowal, and indeed his whole universe, would behold a new and more understandable revelation of the Father of all.
ch00.b009: The security of Nebadon would not be his burden. A mandate of the Ancients of Days on Uversa had just been communicated, which would prevent all spiritual jeopardy throughout the period of the bestowal. Rebellion, such as had three times occurred in Nebadon, could not occur while he was away; any being presuming to instigate insurrection would meet instantaneous and automatic extinction. “⟦Q 120:1.5⟧You may proceed upon your mission,⟦/Q⟧” Immanuel said, “⟦Q 120:1.5⟧with but a single thought—the enhanced revelation of our Father to the intelligent beings of your universe.⟦/Q⟧” And all the authority Michael was laying down remained his to take up again at any moment; his bestowal was, throughout, wholly voluntary.
ch00.b010: Then Immanuel set out his counsel. Michael was to grow up on Urantia as a child of the realm and complete his human education, all the while subject to the will of his Paradise Father. After he became sufficiently self-conscious of his divine identity, he was to undertake, as the Son of Man, the task of technically terminating the Lucifer rebellion, achieving in weakness made powerful by faith what he had repeatedly declined to accomplish by power and might. To the generation of men among whom he would live he was to function largely as a teacher: “⟦Q 120:2.5⟧Give attention, first, to the liberation and inspiration of man’s spiritual nature. Next, illuminate the darkened human intellect, heal the souls of men, and emancipate their minds from age-old fears.⟦/Q⟧” His life was to be lived not as an example for the mortals of any one world or age, but as the inspiration for all lives upon all Nebadon worlds throughout all the ages to come. And his great mission was twofold: to reveal God to man, and to make a new revelation of man to God—to show “⟦Q 120:2.8⟧the achievement of God seeking man and finding him and the phenomenon of man seeking God and finding him,⟦/Q⟧” and to do it all during one short lifetime in the flesh.
ch00.b011: There was lesser counsel, arrived at in consultation with Gabriel. He was to give precedence to the accepted customs of family life in the day and generation of his bestowal. He was to avoid all entanglements with the economic structure and the political commitments of his time, and under no circumstances to interfere with the normal evolution of the Urantia races. He might identify himself with existing religious movements, but he was to seek in every possible way to avoid the founding of an organized cult or a crystallized religion: “⟦Q 120:3.6⟧Your life and teachings are to become the common heritage of all religions and all peoples.⟦/Q⟧” He was to leave no writings behind him on the planet, to write nothing upon permanent materials, and to enjoin his associates to make no images or likenesses of him in the flesh, so that nothing potentially idolatrous would remain when he departed. He would probably not enter the marriage relation—a relation wholly honorable and consistent with his bestowal—for a mandate of Sonarington forbade a bestowal Son of Paradise origin to leave human offspring behind on any planet.
ch00.b012: And Immanuel added a caution. While in fact Michael was to become an ordinary human of the realm, in potential he would remain a Creator Son; the creative attributes of his divinity would follow him from Salvington to Urantia. Before the arrival of his Thought Adjuster, Immanuel would vouch for his personality integrity. After it, he must himself refrain from forming any superhuman will to attainment or power. In all other details he was committed to the leading of the indwelling Adjuster, the teaching of the ever-present divine spirit of human guidance, and the reason-judgment of his expanding human mind. Such an association of creature and Creator, Immanuel said, would enable him to live the perfect life of man—“⟦Q 120:3.9⟧not necessarily perfect as regarded by any one man in any one generation on any one world (much less on Urantia) but wholly and supremely replete⟦/Q⟧” as judged on the more perfect worlds of his universe.
ch00.b013: Last of all came the blessing, and the farewell.
ch00.b015: Then, immediately, in the presence of all Salvington assembled, Michael removed himself from their midst. His accustomed place stood empty, and they saw him there no more until he returned as the supreme and personal ruler of the universe, his bestowal career on Urantia complete.
ch00.b017: How it was done remained a mystery even to the beings of the universe. To those who live as citizens of a local universe there are few miracles, but of these by far the most intriguing are the incarnational bestowals of the Paradise Sons. The appearance on a world, by apparently natural processes, of a divine Son they regard as a miracle, the operation of universal laws beyond their understanding. Jesus of Nazareth was a miraculous person.
ch00.b018: Yet there must be no mistake. Christ Michael, while truly a dual-origin being, was not a double personality. He was not God in association with man but, rather, God incarnate in man. He did not progressively become God, and God did not, at some vital moment in the earth life of Jesus, become man. Jesus was God and man—always and even forevermore. The only thing that grew in that relationship was the human mind’s progressive realization and recognition of this fact of being God and man. And through all of it, God the Father chose to manifest himself as he always does, “⟦Q 120:4.6⟧in the normal, natural, and dependable way of divine acting.⟦/Q⟧”
ch00.b019: Never was the supreme spiritual purpose of the bestowal to be lost from sight: it was to enhance the revelation of God. Those children of Michael who had once accused their Creator of selfishly seeking rulership would be silenced forever by the life of self-forgetful service that the Son of God now entered upon as the Son of Man.
ch00.b021: Jesus did not come to the world in an age of spiritual decadence. At the time of his birth Urantia was experiencing such a revival of spiritual thinking and religious living as it had not known in all its post-Adamic history, nor has known since. Never before or after did the world present a more favorable condition for a Creator Son’s bestowal.
ch00.b022: The whole Mediterranean world was one unified empire. For the first time in history good roads connected many of the great centers; the seas had been cleared of pirates, and a great era of trade and travel was advancing. Three influences bound that civilization together: Roman political and social systems, the Greek language and culture, and the rapidly spreading influence of Jewish religious and moral teaching. Paul would one day embody all three—a Hebrew of the Hebrews proclaiming a Jewish Messiah in the Greek tongue, himself a Roman citizen. Beneath the peace and surface prosperity, however, most of the empire’s inhabitants languished in squalor and poverty. A small upper class was rich; half the population were slaves; a happy and prosperous middle class had only begun to appear.
ch00.b023: At the heart of that world lay Palestine. The travel, trade, and armies of Babylonia, Assyria, Egypt, Syria, Greece, Parthia, and Rome had swept over it in turn, for it was the crossroads of three continents. From time immemorial caravan routes from the Orient had passed through the region to the few good seaports at the eastern end of the Mediterranean, and more than half of this caravan traffic passed through or near the little town of Nazareth in Galilee. Meanwhile the Jews were abroad in every province of the Roman and Parthian states. Greece provided a language and a culture, Rome built the roads, but the dispersion of the Jews, with their more than two hundred synagogues scattered throughout the Roman world, would provide the centers in which the new gospel of the kingdom of heaven first found reception, and from which it spread to the uttermost parts of the earth. Wherever they lived, the Jews kept their hearts turned toward the temple at Jerusalem, and as many as two and one-half million of them used to come up to the city for the great festivals.
ch00.b024: Three languages were spoken in the land. The common people used some dialect of Aramaic; the priests and rabbis spoke Hebrew; the educated classes spoke Greek. The early translation of the Hebrew scriptures into Greek at Alexandria had joined Jewish faith to the wide Greek-speaking world. Herod built the harbor of Caesarea and made Palestine still more the crossroads of the civilized world. He died in 4 B.C., and his son Herod Antipas, a great builder like his father, governed Galilee and Perea throughout Jesus’ youth and ministry, until A.D. 39, rebuilding many Galilean cities, among them the important trade center of Sepphoris.
ch00.b026: The Jews of that day, though under Roman suzerainty, enjoyed a considerable degree of self-government. They remembered the heroic deliverance won by Judas Maccabee and his successors, and they were vibrant with the expectation of a still greater deliverer, the long-expected Messiah. Yet they were unusually apprehensive and suspicious, because they were ruled by an outsider, Herod the Idumean, who professed loyalty to the Hebrew ceremonies while building temples for many strange gods. The religious leaders and rabbis of Jerusalem did not regard the Galileans with full favor; when Jesus was born, Galilee was more gentile than Jewish.
ch00.b027: The Jews had built up a rigid wall of separation between themselves and the gentile world. They worshiped the letter of the law, and the spoken interpretations of the scribes had become a higher authority than the written law itself, pursuing every loyal Jew into every corner of personal and social life. Most of them pictured a Messiah who would come as part of their national and racial history. They were unwilling to share Yahweh on equal terms with the gentiles. Jeremiah had told of a “⟦Q 121:7.5⟧law to be written in men’s hearts,⟦/Q⟧” and Ezekiel of a “⟦Q 121:7.5⟧new spirit to live in man’s soul,⟦/Q⟧” but tradition had grown into fetters they could not break.
ch00.b028: The gentile world, too, was hungry. The Epicureans pursued happiness; the Stoics taught a lofty morality of reason and virtue and called themselves the “offspring of God,” yet failed to know him; the wandering Cynic preachers went through fields and market places proclaiming that “⟦Q 121:4.4⟧man could save himself if he would.⟦/Q⟧” But these were philosophies for the strong and the wise, not religions of salvation for the poor and the weak. Into the empty place a flood of mystery cults had broken, new and strange religions from the Levant that promised the common people “⟦Q 121:5.11⟧deliverance from evil, survival after death, and enduring life in blissful realms beyond this world of sorrow and slavery.⟦/Q⟧” Their popularity revealed a real hunger and thirst for personal religion. They could not satisfy it, but they prepared the way for one who truly brought to the world the bread of life and the water thereof.
ch00.b029: It was an enchanted age. Many believed that every rock and tree was possessed by spirits, good or bad, and everybody believed in miracles as commonplace occurrences. Into such a generation of men, dominated by incomplete systems of philosophy and perplexed by complex cults of religion, Jesus was born in Palestine. And to this same generation he later gave his gospel of personal religion—sonship with God.
ch00.b031: After he had gone, men wrote his story down, though slowly, for they knew how carefully the Master had refused to put his teachings in writing. John Mark wrote the earliest and simplest account, in reality the Gospel according to Simon Peter, completing it near the end of A.D. 68. Isador, a disciple of the Apostle Matthew, wrote for Jewish Christians at Pella in the year 71, drawing on his teacher’s memories and notes. Luke, the physician of Antioch in Pisidia and a gentile convert of Paul, wrote in Achaia in the year 82 and presented the Master as “⟦Q 121:8.8⟧the friend of publicans and sinners.⟦/Q⟧” And John, seeing how much the other records had omitted, encouraged his associate Nathan in A.D. 101 to begin writing the narrative that bears his name.
ch00.b032: The Apostle Andrew also kept a record. But knowing how scrupulously his Master had avoided leaving written records behind him, Andrew steadfastly refused to multiply copies of it, and it was lost. All these writers presented honest pictures of Jesus as they saw, remembered, or had learned of him. Imperfect as their records are, they have been sufficient to change the course of the history of Urantia for almost two thousand years.
ch00.b033: What follows is that story told again from its beginning: how a decision made in heaven became a life lived on earth. It begins, as all such stories must, in an ordinary house, with a carpenter and his young wife in Galilee, and with news neither of them could have imagined.
part1: Part One: The Child of Nazareth
ch01.title: Gabriel's Visit
ch01.b002: Once Michael had chosen Urantia, Gabriel came to the world in person. He studied its human groups and surveyed the spiritual, intellectual, racial, and geographic features of its peoples, and he concluded that the Hebrews possessed those relative advantages which warranted their selection as the bestowal race. When Michael approved, Gabriel appointed the Family Commission of Twelve, chosen from among the higher orders of universe personalities, and sent them to investigate Jewish family life. When the commission finished its labors, Gabriel himself was present on Urantia to receive their report. It named three prospective unions, all, in the commission’s opinion, equally favorable as bestowal families. From these three couples Gabriel made his personal choice: Joseph and Mary of Nazareth in Galilee.
ch01.b003: Joseph was a Hebrew of the Hebrews, though many non-Jewish strains had entered his family tree through the female lines. His ancestry went back to the days of Abraham, yet David and Solomon were not in his direct line. His immediate forebears were mechanics—builders, carpenters, masons, and smiths—and Joseph himself was a carpenter. His family belonged to a long line of the nobility of the common people. Mary’s inheritance was wider still. Among her ancestors were such well-known women as Tamar, Ruth, and Bathsheba, and no Jewish woman of her day had a more illustrious lineage of common progenitors. In culture and belief she was a Jew, but in hereditary endowment she was more a composite of Syrian, Hittite, Phoenician, Greek, and Egyptian stocks. And yet she was an average woman of her day and generation, of a fairly normal temperament.
ch01.b004: That, in the end, was the reason for the choice. It was Michael’s plan to appear on earth as an average man, that the common people might understand him and receive him. Of all couples living in Palestine at that time, Joseph and Mary possessed the most ideal combination of widespread racial connections and superior average of personality endowments. Gabriel looked for no princes. He chose just such persons as Joseph and Mary.
ch01.b006: Their story had begun simply. When Joseph was a young man, he was employed by Mary’s father to build an addition to his house, and one day at the noontime meal Mary brought him a cup of water. With that cup of water the courtship of the pair who were destined to become the parents of Jesus really began. Almost two years later, when Joseph was twenty-one, they were married in accordance with Jewish custom at Mary’s home in the environs of Nazareth. The wedding took place in March, 8 B.C.
ch01.b007: Joseph was a mild-mannered man, extremely conscientious and in every way faithful to the religious practices of his people. He talked little but thought much, and the sorry plight of the Jewish people caused him much sadness. Mary’s temperament was quite the opposite. She was usually cheerful, very rarely downcast, and of an ever-sunny disposition, expressing her feelings freely and often. He was a thinker; she was a planner, expert in adaptation and practical in immediate execution. Joseph was a black-eyed brunet; Mary, a brown-eyed, well-nigh blond type. Both had been educated far above the average for their day and station in life.
ch01.b008: They differed, too, in how they pictured the coming deliverer. Joseph held vigorously to the Eastern, or Babylonian, views of the Jewish religion and leaned toward a spiritual concept of the Messiah. Mary leaned toward the broader Western, or Hellenistic, interpretation of the law and the prophets, yet in the matter of the Messiah she and her family, especially her father, held to the idea of a temporal deliverer and political ruler; her ancestors had been prominent in the Maccabean struggles of recent times. In years to come the larger part of Joseph’s family would believe in the teachings of Jesus, but very few of Mary’s people believed in him until after he had left this world.
ch01.b009: The child would draw on them both. From his father he would derive much of his unusual gentleness and his marvelous sympathetic understanding of human nature; from his mother, his gift as a great teacher and his tremendous capacity for righteous indignation. From Joseph he would receive strict training in the Jewish ceremonials and an unusual acquaintance with the Hebrew scriptures; from Mary, a broader view of religious life and a more liberal concept of personal spiritual freedom.
ch01.b010: Elizabeth in the City of Judah
ch01.b011: Late in June, 8 B.C., about three months after Joseph and Mary were married, Gabriel appeared at noontide to Elizabeth in the City of Judah. She belonged to the more prosperous branch of the same large family to which Mary belonged, and her husband, Zacharias, was a priest. They had been married many years and were childless. Gabriel said:
ch01.b013: The vision greatly frightened Elizabeth. After Gabriel had gone she turned the experience over in her mind, long pondering the words of the majestic visitor, and for five months she withheld the secret even from her husband. When at last she told him, Zacharias was very skeptical. For weeks he doubted the whole matter and only halfheartedly consented to believe it when he could no longer question that his wife was expecting a child. He was much perplexed by her coming motherhood, given his own advanced age, but he never doubted her integrity.
ch01.b015: About the middle of November, 8 B.C., one evening about sundown, before Joseph had come home from his work, Gabriel appeared to Mary by the side of a low stone table in their Nazareth home. When she had recovered her composure, he said:
ch01.b017: The announcement came on the day following the conception of Jesus, and it was the only event of supernatural occurrence connected with Mary’s entire experience of carrying and bearing the child of promise.
ch01.b018: For many weeks Mary pondered the visitation secretly in her heart. Only when she knew of a certainty that she was with child did she dare to tell her husband. Joseph had great confidence in Mary, but when he heard it all he was much troubled and could not sleep for many nights. At first he doubted the visitation. Then, when he became nearly persuaded that Mary had really heard the voice and seen the form of the divine messenger, he was torn in mind over how such things could be. How could the offspring of human beings be a child of divine destiny? Only after several weeks of thought did the two of them reach the conclusion that they had been chosen to become the parents of the Messiah, though it had hardly been the Jewish idea that the expected deliverer would be of divine nature.
ch01.b019: Having come to this conclusion, Mary hastened to visit Elizabeth in the City of Judah, four miles west of Jerusalem in the hills. Gabriel had told each mother-to-be of his appearance to the other, and they were eager to compare their experiences and talk over the futures of their sons. Mary stayed with her distant cousin three weeks, and Elizabeth did much to strengthen her faith, so that she returned home more fully dedicated to mothering the child of destiny. Afterward she visited her parents, Joachim and Hannah. Her parents, her two brothers, and her two sisters knew nothing of Gabriel, and they would always be skeptical of Jesus’ divine mission. But to her sister Salome Mary confided that she thought her son was destined to become a great teacher.
ch01.b021: What finally reconciled Joseph to the idea that Mary was to become the mother of an extraordinary child was a very impressive dream. In it a brilliant celestial messenger appeared to him and, among other things, said:
ch01.b023: After that, Joseph never again wholly doubted Mary’s story.
ch01.b024: In none of these visitations was anything said about the house of David. Nothing was ever intimated about the child’s becoming a “deliverer of the Jews,” not even that he was to be the long-expected Messiah. Jesus was not such a Messiah as the Jews anticipated, but he was the world’s deliverer, and his mission was to all races and peoples. Joseph, in fact, was not of the line of King David; Mary had more of the Davidic ancestry than he. Six generations earlier an orphaned forefather of Joseph had been adopted by one Zadoc, a direct descendant of David, and for that reason Joseph was also accounted as of the “house of David.” Many of the so-called Messianic prophecies were applied to Jesus only long after his life on earth had been lived. Even the passage “⟦Q 122:4.4⟧a maiden shall bear a son⟦/Q⟧” was made to read “⟦Q 122:4.4⟧a virgin shall bear a son.⟦/Q⟧”
ch01.b025: The Stone House Below the Hill
ch01.b026: Zacharias’s last doubts were also removed by a dream. About six weeks before his son’s birth he had an impressive dream, and from then on he was fully convinced that Elizabeth was to become the mother of a son of destiny, one who would prepare the way for the Messiah. John was born in the City of Judah on March 25, 7 B.C. Zacharias and Elizabeth rejoiced greatly that a son had come to them as Gabriel had promised, and on the eighth day, when they presented the child for circumcision, they formally named him John. A nephew of Zacharias had already set out for Nazareth, carrying Elizabeth’s message to Mary that a son had been born to her and that his name was to be John.
ch01.b027: In Nazareth the young couple waited in their new home. Joseph had built it with the help of two of his brothers. It stood in the outskirts of the town, near the foot of the high hill in the northern part of Nazareth, some distance from the village spring on the eastern side, about midway between the base of the hill and the road leading out toward Cana. From there the elevated land charmingly overlooked the surrounding countryside.
ch01.b028: It was a one-room stone structure with a flat roof and an adjoining building for the animals. The furnishings were few: a low stone table, earthenware and stone dishes and pots, a loom, a lampstand, several small stools, and mats for sleeping on the stone floor. In the back yard, near the animal shelter, a roof covered the oven and the mill for grinding grain, a mill that took two people to work it, one to grind and another to feed in the grain. Mary was an expert weaver, a good housekeeper and a superior homemaker.
ch01.b029: In this home, especially prepared, the young parents had thought to welcome the child of promise. They little realized that this momentous event of a universe would take place while they were far from home, in Bethlehem of Judea.
ch02.title: The Night in Bethlehem
ch02.b002: Orders from Rome reached even the small towns of Galilee, slowly but surely. In March, 8 B.C., the very month Joseph and Mary were married, Caesar Augustus had decreed that all the inhabitants of the Roman Empire should be numbered, so that a census could be used for better taxation. Throughout the rest of the empire the registration was made that same year. But the Jews had always been greatly prejudiced against any attempt to “number the people,” and this, together with the serious domestic troubles of Herod, King of Judea, delayed the census in the Jewish kingdom for one year. In Herod’s Palestine it was taken in 7 B.C. Joseph, accounted as of the “house of David,” was to be registered at Bethlehem, the City of David, far to the south in Judea.
ch02.b003: It was not necessary for Mary to go. Joseph was authorized to register for his whole family. But Mary was an adventurous and aggressive person, and she insisted on accompanying him. She was afraid of being left alone, lest the child be born while Joseph was away. And Bethlehem was not far from the City of Judah, so she foresaw the pleasure of a visit with her kinswoman Elizabeth. Joseph virtually forbade her to come, but it was of no avail. When the food was packed for a trip of three or four days, she prepared double rations and made herself ready for the road. Before they set out, Joseph had made his peace with her going along.
ch02.b004: They were poor. Building and furnishing the house had been a great drain on Joseph, who also had to help support his parents, since his father had recently been disabled. They had only one beast of burden. So Mary, large with child, rode the animal with the provisions while Joseph walked ahead, leading it. Early on the morning of August 18, 7 B.C., at the break of day, this Jewish couple went forth cheerfully from their humble home in Nazareth on the road to Bethlehem.
ch02.b005: The First Night by the Jordan
ch02.b006: The first day’s journey carried them around the foothills of Mount Gilboa and down to the river Jordan, where they made camp for the night. In the dusk, with the low sound of the river beside them, the two talked for a long time, and their talk kept returning to one subject: what sort of son would be born to them. Joseph held to the idea of a spiritual teacher. Mary held to the idea of a Jewish Messiah, a deliverer of the Hebrew nation. Neither persuaded the other. The night came down over the valley, and the stars stood out above the water, and they lay down at last with the question still open between them.
ch02.b007: It was an old difference, and an honest one. Joseph had always leaned toward the spiritual concept of the expected Messiah, and Mary, like her father, toward a temporal deliverer. Each carried, in a different way, the hope of a whole people. Joseph, mild and conscientious, grieved over the sorry plight of the Jewish people and looked for a teacher who would lift their spirits; Mary, cheerful and determined, and descended from those prominent in the Maccabean struggles, looked for a deliverer who would lift their yoke. Neither could yet imagine that the child would be a deliverer of a kind no one had expected, and that his mission would reach beyond the Hebrew nation to all races and peoples.
ch02.b009: Bright and early on the morning of August 19 they were on their way again. At noon they ate their meal at the foot of Mount Sartaba, overlooking the Jordan valley, with the river running south below them like a green ribbon through the dry land. Then they went on, and by evening they had reached Jericho, where they stopped at an inn on the highway in the outskirts of the city.
ch02.b010: After the evening meal there was much talk among the travelers. They discussed the oppressiveness of Roman rule, and Herod, and the census enrollment, and the comparative influence of Jerusalem and Alexandria as centers of Jewish learning and culture. Joseph took part in the conversation, and among those he talked with that evening was a man whom he would meet again, unexpectedly, two days later. When the talk was done the travelers from Nazareth retired for the night.
ch02.b011: Early on the morning of August 20 they resumed their journey, climbing up from the deep valley toward the hills of Judea. Before noon they reached Jerusalem and visited the temple. Then they went on to the south, and in midafternoon they arrived at Bethlehem.
ch02.b013: Bethlehem was full. The inn was overcrowded, and so Joseph went looking for lodging with distant relatives, but every room in Bethlehem was filled to overflowing. Tired and anxious, he returned to the courtyard of the inn. There he was told that the caravan stables, hewn out of the side of the rock just below the inn, had been cleared of animals and cleaned up for the reception of lodgers.
ch02.b014: Leaving the donkey in the courtyard, Joseph shouldered their bags of clothing and provisions and went down the stone steps with Mary to their lodging below. They found themselves in what had been a grain storage room in front of the stalls and mangers. Tent curtains had been hung to make a kind of chamber, and they counted themselves fortunate to have such comfortable quarters. The cool of the rock surrounded them, and the noise of the crowded town came down only faintly from above.
ch02.b015: Joseph had meant to go out at once and enroll. But Mary was weary. She was considerably distressed, and she begged him to stay by her side. He did.
ch02.b017: All that night Mary was restless, and neither of them slept much. By the break of day the pangs of childbirth were well in evidence. Women among their fellow travelers came to help, and with their kind ministrations, at noon on August 21, 7 B.C., Mary was delivered of a male child. Jesus of Nazareth was born into the world. He was wrapped in the clothes that Mary had brought along against just such a possibility, and laid in a near-by manger.
ch02.b018: In just the same manner as all babies before that day and since have come into the world, the promised child was born. There was nothing to set him apart from any other newborn infant of the realm: a small, warm body, a first cry, a mother’s exhausted joy. On the eighth day, according to Jewish practice, he was circumcised and formally named Joshua—Jesus.
ch02.b019: Yet the birth was not unattended. At that noontide hour the seraphim of Urantia, assembled under their directors, sang anthems of glory over the Bethlehem manger. But these utterances of praise were not heard by human ears. No shepherds and no other mortal creatures came that day to pay homage to the babe of Bethlehem. Above, in the courtyard of the inn, the ordinary business of a crowded town went on, and in the room beneath it, in the rock, a Creator Son lay sleeping in a manger.
ch02.b020: The Room at the Inn and Zacharias’s Conviction
ch02.b021: The day after Jesus was born, Joseph went out to make his enrollment. While he was about it, he met the man he had talked with two nights before at Jericho. This man took Joseph to a well-to-do friend who had a room at the inn, and the friend said he would gladly exchange quarters with the couple from Nazareth. That afternoon they moved up into the inn. They lived there almost three weeks, until they found lodgings in the home of a distant relative of Joseph.
ch02.b022: On the second day after the birth, Mary sent word to Elizabeth that her child had come. Word came back inviting Joseph up to Jerusalem to talk over all their affairs with Zacharias, and the following week he went. Both Zacharias and Elizabeth had come to the sincere conviction that Jesus was indeed to be the Jewish deliverer, the Messiah, and that their son John was to be his chief of aides, his right-hand man of destiny. Mary held the same ideas. So it was not difficult to persuade Joseph to remain in Bethlehem, the City of David, so that Jesus might grow up to become the successor of David on the throne of all Israel. They stayed in Bethlehem more than a year, and Joseph meanwhile worked some at his carpenter’s trade.
ch02.b023: So the plan of the household changed. The home in Nazareth, built with such care and furnished at such cost, stood empty in the north, while the little family settled into the life of a strange town in Judea. The hopes of the two families were now bound together: in the City of Judah a small boy named John, five months older than Jesus, was beginning his life under parents who already believed he would stand at the right hand of the Messiah. Zacharias, the priest, had become the counselor of the young couple, and his confidence carried them along. Joseph alone kept something of his own quieter view, that his son was to be a spiritual teacher rather than a king.
ch02.b025: When the baby was almost three weeks old, strangers came to see him. They were three priests from Ur in Mesopotamia. Some time before, a strange religious teacher of their country had told them of a dream in which he was informed that “the light of life” was about to appear on earth as a babe, among the Jews. And so these three teachers had come west looking for this “light of life.” For many weeks they searched in vain in Jerusalem, and they were about to go home to Ur when Zacharias met them. He disclosed his belief that Jesus was the object of their quest and sent them on to Bethlehem. There they found the babe, and they left their gifts with Mary, his earth mother.
ch02.b026: These wise men saw no star to guide them to Bethlehem. The beautiful legend of the star came about in another way. On May 29, 7 B.C., there occurred an extraordinary conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn in the constellation of Pisces, and it is a remarkable astronomic fact that similar conjunctions occurred on September 29 and December 5 of the same year. Upon the basis of these extraordinary but wholly natural events, well-meaning zealots of the following generation constructed the appealing legend of the star of Bethlehem and the adoring Magi led by it to the manger. Oriental and near-Oriental minds delight in such stories and are continually spinning beautiful myths about the lives of their religious leaders and political heroes. In an age without printing, when most knowledge was passed by word of mouth, it was very easy for myths to become traditions, and for traditions at last to be accepted as facts.
ch02.b028: Moses had taught the Jews that every first-born son belonged to the Lord. Instead of sacrificing him, as the heathen nations did, his parents might redeem him by the payment of five shekels to any authorized priest. There was also a Mosaic ordinance directing that a mother, after a set time, should present herself at the temple for purification. The two ceremonies were customarily performed together, and so Joseph and Mary went up to the temple in Jerusalem in person, to present Jesus to the priests and redeem him, and to make the proper sacrifice for Mary’s purification. Joseph counted himself poor enough to offer for her two young pigeons, as Moses had directed for the poor.
ch02.b029: Two remarkable characters lingered constantly about the temple courts: Simeon, a singer, and Anna, a poetess. Simeon was a Judean; Anna was a Galilean. They were often together, and both were intimates of the priest Zacharias, who had confided to them the secret of John and Jesus. Both longed for the coming of the Messiah, and their trust in Zacharias led them to believe that Jesus was the expected deliverer. Zacharias knew the day Joseph and Mary would appear with Jesus, and he had arranged to show Simeon and Anna, by the salute of his upraised hand, which child in the procession of first-born was the one.
ch02.b030: For the occasion Anna had written a poem, and Simeon sang it, to the astonishment of Joseph and Mary and of everyone gathered in the temple courts. This was their hymn of the redemption of the first-born son:
ch02.b054: On the way back to Bethlehem Joseph and Mary were silent, confused and overawed. Mary was much disturbed by the farewell salutation of Anna, the aged poetess. Joseph was not in harmony with this premature effort to make Jesus out to be the expected Messiah of the Jewish people. What had been sung in the temple courts had been heard by many, and a song is not easily recalled once it has been sung. Neither of them could know how soon it would reach the ears of the king.
ch02.b056: Joseph had reason for unease. Herod’s watchers were not idle. When they reported the visit of the priests of Ur to Bethlehem, Herod summoned these Chaldeans before him and questioned them diligently about the new “king of the Jews.” They gave him little satisfaction. The babe, they explained, had been born of a woman who had come down to Bethlehem with her husband for the census. Herod was not satisfied. He sent them away with a purse and directed them to find the child, so that he too might come and worship him, since they had declared that the child’s kingdom was to be spiritual, not temporal. But the wise men did not return, and Herod grew suspicious.
ch02.b057: While he was turning these things over in his mind, his informers came back with a full report of what had happened in the temple. They even brought him a copy of parts of the song Simeon had sung at the redemption ceremony. But they had failed to follow Joseph and Mary, and when they could not tell him where the pair had taken the child, Herod was very angry. He dispatched searchers to find them. Knowing that Herod was pursuing the family from Nazareth, Zacharias and Elizabeth stayed away from Bethlehem, and the baby boy was hidden with Joseph’s relatives.
ch02.b058: Those were anxious months. Joseph was afraid to look for work, and their small savings were rapidly disappearing. The child passed his first birthday in hiding, and still Herod’s spies searched.
ch02.b060: After more than a year of searching, Herod’s spies had still not found Jesus. Suspecting that the child was still hidden in Bethlehem, Herod prepared an order: every house in Bethlehem was to be searched systematically, and all boy babies under two years of age were to be killed. In this way he hoped to make sure that the child who was to become “king of the Jews” would be destroyed. Intrigue and murder, even within his own family, were common occurrences at Herod’s court.
ch02.b061: But there were believers in the coming Messiah even among Herod’s court attachés. One of them learned of the order and got word to Zacharias, and Zacharias at once sent a messenger to Joseph. The night before the massacre, Joseph and Mary left Bethlehem in the dark with their child, bound for Alexandria in Egypt. To avoid attracting attention they traveled alone. Zacharias provided the funds for the journey.
ch02.b062: The next day, about the middle of October, 6 B.C., the order was carried out, and sixteen boy babies perished in one day in Bethlehem of Judea. Jesus was then a little over one year old, and he was already on the road to Egypt.
